title: From exploration to dispersion, and beyond
summary: How collaborative exploration asks how much a team speeds up a search, how dispersion arose as the case k = n under weaker assumptions, what dispersion gives back to exploration, and why dispersing first has become the standard opening move for computing graph structures with agents.

sections.heading: Exploring together
sections.body:
Fraigniaud, Gąsieniec, Kowalski and Pelc posed collective tree exploration: $k$ agents start at the root of an unknown tree and must visit every node as fast as possible [Fraigniaud2006Collective]. The offline optimum is $\Theta(n/k + D)$, by spreading the agents along an Euler tour of the tree [Disser2020General]. Their algorithm is $O(k/\log k)$-competitive, which Disser, Mousset, Noever, Škorić and Steger call "only slightly better than the trivial upper bound of $O(k)$" of a single depth-first traversal [Disser2020General] [Fraigniaud2006Collective]; without any information sharing, a factor $k$ is unavoidable [Fraigniaud2006Collective]. Cosson, Massoulié and Viennot frame the problem as "a fundamental problem behind the exploration of an unknown physical environment with a team of agents" and add: "Despite almost two decades of research, we still do not completely understand how much exploration time can decrease with the number of agents" [Cosson2023BFDN].

The lower bound side was opened by Dynia, Łopuszański and Schindelhauer, who showed $\Omega(\log k/\log\log k)$ for $k < \sqrt n$ (as reported by [Disser2020General]); Disser et al. extended it to $k \le n\log^\kappa n$ for every constant $\kappa$ [Disser2020General]. The upper bound moved from $O(k/\log k)$ to below $k/\log k$ [Cosson2024Mining], to $O(\sqrt k)$ [Cosson2024Potential], and in a 2026 preprint to $O(\log^2 k)$ [Cosson2026Polylog]. These results assume labelled nodes and, except in the whiteboard variants, free communication, so the agents share a map of what has been explored.

sections.heading: Teams with little memory
sections.body:
A second line asks what a team can do with very little memory, and here agents act as markers for each other. Rollik's traps show that no finite team of finite automata explores all graphs [Rollik1980Planar] (as recounted by [Disser2019Pebbles]). Disser, Hackfeld and Klimm observe that a team of $p+1$ agents can simulate one agent with $p$ pebbles, one agent walking while the others stand still, and that before their work no algorithm explored undirected graphs with sublogarithmic memory using several agents or pebbles [Disser2019Pebbles]. Their result closes the question:

> "Since an additional agent is at least as powerful as a pebble, this implies that $O(\log\log n)$ agents with constant memory can explore any $n$-vertex graph." [Disser2019Pebbles]

They also show that $\Omega(\log\log n)$ agents are needed even when each has $O((\log n)^{1-\varepsilon})$ bits [Disser2019Pebbles]. An agent that stays still is a marker; dispersion is built on the same idea.

sections.heading: Dispersion as exploration with k = n
sections.body:
Augustine and Moses Jr. introduced dispersion in 2018: $k$ agents on an $n$-node graph must reach a configuration with at most one agent per node. Their motivation is self-driving electric cars that look for free charging stations instead of queueing, and they place the problem between scattering, exploration and load balancing from the first page [Augustine2018Tradeoffs]:

> "Since any solution to a problem of dispersion acts as a solution to $n$ robot exploration under the same conditions, any possibility results achieved for dispersion apply to $n$ robot exploration." [Augustine2018Tradeoffs]

Lower bounds move the other way, so the $\Omega(D^2)$ bound for $n$ agents on trees [Disser2020General] is a dispersion lower bound. The catalogue records that this bound is existential in $D$ (the hard trees have height about $\sqrt{\log n}$), so whether rooted dispersion on taller trees needs $\Omega(D^2)$ rounds is open.

The assumptions are much weaker than in collaborative exploration. Sudo, Shibata, Nakamura, Kim and Masuzawa single out "the unique computation model": no node identifiers, no memory at the nodes, agents with identifiers that talk only when they share a node [Sudo2024NearLinear]. The algorithms recover the marker idea: in the depth-first dispersion of Kshemkalyani and Ali, "A robot that docks at a node helps other robots to determine whether they have visited this node before" [Kshemkalyani2019Efficient]. Every later improvement up to time-optimal $O(k)$ rounds with $O(\log(k+\Delta))$ bits, synchronous [Kshemkalyani2025Almost] and asynchronous [Pattanayak2025OptimalAsync], is a faster way of using settled agents as markers on anonymous nodes.

sections.heading: What dispersion gives back
sections.body:
Because dispersion with $k = n$ explores, the dispersion results are also the best known results for $n$ agents exploring an anonymous graph with only local communication: $O(n)$ rounds and $O(\log n)$ bits per agent from a rooted start [Kshemkalyani2025Almost], an inference the catalogue makes and the paper does not state. With labelled nodes and global communication, $n$ agents explore a tree in $D^2$ rounds [Disser2020General]; whether anonymity and local communication force $\Omega(n)$ rounds on shallow trees is open, and Augustine and Moses Jr. already asked for $o(n)$-round dispersion on trees [Augustine2018Tradeoffs].

Dispersion also gave exploration-type questions new resources to measure. Gorain, Mandal and Mondal took up the question of Bouchard, Dieudonné and Pelc whether gathering needs communication [Bouchard2023Chatter] and asked it for dispersion: their silent agents convey information only by the timing of moves and by counts of co-located agents [Gorain2022Silent]. Molla and Moses Jr. replaced identifiers by coin flips [Molla2019Randomness]. Each such variant is, for $k = n$, a statement about collaborative exploration under the same assumptions.

sections.heading: Dispersion as a primitive for computing with agents
sections.body:
Kshemkalyani, Kumar, Molla and Sharma describe the agent-based model by its two differences from message passing: the nodes have no identifiers, computation or storage, and devices can exchange information only when co-located, so a message to a neighbour requires a move [Kshemkalyani2024AgentLE]. With $n$ agents on $n$ nodes the model corresponds to message passing with one device per node, and their simulation theorem converts any message-passing algorithm that runs in $R$ rounds into an $O(\Delta R\log n)$-round agent algorithm from a dispersed start (plus $O(n\log^2 n)$ rounds otherwise), provided $n$ and $\Delta$ are known [Kshemkalyani2024AgentLE]. Their stated goal is to remove that knowledge, and they note that limited storage "makes it impossible for the relocatable devices to first traverse the graph to learn the topology and then run graph computation as a second step" [Kshemkalyani2024AgentLE].

Dispersion is the first step in most of what followed. Chand, Molla and Sivasubramaniam built dominating sets on it: "Our algorithms rely on the ideas used for dispersion", taking "advantage of the fact that most dispersion protocols involve the exploration of $G$" [Chand2023Cover]. For triangle counting, Chand, Das and Molla state that a dispersed configuration "is a requirement" [Chand2026Triangle]. Kaur, Gorain and Mondal reach maximal independent sets through distance-2 dispersion, which with $n$ agents is the same problem, and elect a leader on the way [Kaur2026MIS]. Chand and Molla build on time-optimal dispersion [Kshemkalyani2025Almost] to obtain, in $O(n)$ rounds, termination after dispersion, a spanning tree, a leader and a minimal dominating set [Chand2026MDS].

The progress is quick. Leader election without knowledge went from $O(m)$ rounds with $O(n\log n)$ bits [Kshemkalyani2024AgentLE] to $O(n\log^2 n)$ rounds with $O(\log n)$ bits [Kshemkalyani2025NearLinear] and to $O(n)$ rounds [Chand2026MDS]. Maximal independent sets [Pattanayak2024MIS] [Kaur2026MIS], minimum spanning trees and BFS trees [Chand2025Trees], and triangle and butterfly counts [Chand2026Triangle] [Chand2025Butterfly] followed the same route.

sections.heading: Open questions on the boundary
sections.body:
1. **Height versus size.** Is $\Omega(D^2)$ the right bound for $n$ agents on a tree of every height? Exploration theory proves it for one height [Disser2020General]; dispersion uses it for all.
2. **Settled agents versus pebbles.** A pebble is a mute marker; a settled agent stores and exchanges $O(\log n)$ bits. How much of the $\Theta(\log\log n)$ pebble bound [Disser2019Pebbles] changes when markers can talk?
3. **Anonymity versus labels.** The collaborative-exploration bounds assume labelled nodes and global communication; dispersion assumes neither. Where does anonymity start to cost time?
4. **Lower bounds for agent-based problems.** No time lower bound specific to leader election, independent sets, dominating sets or spanning trees by agents is recorded in the catalogue; the only bounds come from dispersion itself. Whether the $O(n)$ rounds of [Chand2026MDS] are optimal for leader election, in particular from a dispersed start where no dispersion is needed, is open.

further: The open questions above are recorded with their variants: the rooted-tree and tree variants of dispersion, and the *anonymous graphs with $k = n$ agents* variant of collaborative exploration.
